Because "temporary spatiotemporal vacuum" is not a single, universally standardized term in physics, its meaning depends entirely on the scientific context you are looking at. It generally refers to a localized area where a vacuum state or negative pressure is applied, generated, or modified across both space and time for a limited duration. 
The phrase typically appears in three major fields: 
1. Quantum Field Theory & High-Intensity Physics
In advanced physics, researchers study the spatiotemporal entanglement of the vacuum or quantum vacuum non-linearities.

Because "temporary spatiotemporal vacuum" is not a single, universally standardized term in physics, its meaning depends entirely on the scientific context you are looking at. It generally refers to a localized area where a vacuum state or negative pressure is applied, generated, or modified across both space and time for a limited duration.
The phrase typically appears in three major fields:
1. Quantum Field Theory & High-Intensity Physics
In advanced physics, researchers study the spatiotemporal entanglement of the vacuum or quantum vacuum non-linearities. 
arXiv.org
 +1
When high-intensity laser pulses collide with X-ray beams at precise, finite spatiotemporal offsets (specific gaps in time and space), they can briefly disturb the quantum vacuum.

This creates a temporary, localized zone where the vacuum behaves non-linearly—essentially allowing scientists to "probe" empty space and watch light scatter off the vacuum itself.

2. Civil Engineering (Vacuum Preloading)
In geotechnical engineering, a literal "temporary spatiotemporal vacuum" is used to stabilize soft soil. 
ACM Digital Library
During vacuum preloading, heavy-duty pumps apply negative pressure underneath a sealed membrane to suck water out of muddy ground.
This vacuum is temporary (lasting around 15 days) and spatiotemporal because the vacuum pressure (V(t, z)) continuously changes over time (t) and depth/space (z) as it moves through different layers of soil.

3. Cosmology & Vacuum Decay
In theoretical physics, space might currently exist in a false vacuum—a temporary, metastable state that looks completely empty but isn't at its lowest possible energy.
